Period schedule:
  Row 1: 45 minutes × 11 periods = 495 minutes
Total: 11 periods · 8h 15min

periods.activity_title: Before We Read: Feathered Friends and Space

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us read — pre-reading (p.205): paired discussion on feathered friends and space.
Let us read — vocabulary warm-up (p.206): complete words by inserting vowels.

time_bands.activity: Open the unit by inviting students to share what they know about birds kept as pets. Pose the pre-reading question from "Let us read" (p.205): who can a feathered friend be, and could one accompany astronauts to space? Take brief responses from pairs.

Move to the vocabulary warm-up from "Let us read" (p.206). Students work in pairs inserting vowels into gapped words — regulation, forbid, fuse, abruptly, confess, dietitian. Elicit answers and write each completed word on the board with a quick pronunciation model.

Read the opening section of "Feathered Friend" aloud — teacher-led with students following in their textbooks (p.205–209). Pause at key moments (Sven smuggling Claribel aboard, Claribel adapting to zero gravity) to check understanding with a quick whole-class question.
Close with a brief pair-share: ask students to say in one sentence what surprised them most about the opening of the story. Take three or four responses to round off the reading.

periods.teacher_notes: The vocabulary warm-up with gapped words is a gentle entry point before the reading — completing "regulation" and "dietitian" prepares students for the station-life setting. A common difficulty is students reading at speed without noticing science-fiction details; deliberate pauses during the read-aloud let the zero-gravity imagery land. The pre-reading discussion on whether animals could accompany astronauts is not assessed here; it serves as an anticipation hook.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.209): four brief-answer questions on Sven's reasons and Claribel's adaptation.
Let us discuss (p.211): true/false statements on Parts I and II events.

time_bands.activity: Continue the read-aloud from where the story was left — the crisis morning when Claribel is found unconscious (p.209–211). Read with expression, modelling the narrator's sluggishness and anxiety.

Work through the brief-answer questions from "Let us discuss" (p.209): Sven's scientific reason for bringing Claribel, how she adapted to the station, and whether her presence might cause trouble. Invite student responses and build discussion around each.
Move to the true/false exercise from "Let us discuss" (p.211). Students judge each statement individually, then share verdicts. Use disagreements to re-read the relevant line from the text aloud.

Consolidate by asking students: in their own words, what is the single most important thing the crew discovered about Claribel in these pages? Take a handful of responses and note the best formulations on the board.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read about Claribel's arrival and adaptation, students now encounter her crisis moment — the shift from mascot to lifesaver begins here. A common pitfall is students treating the true/false statements as guesswork; encourage them to locate the relevant sentence in the text before answering. The question on whether Claribel would cause trouble (p.209) is deliberately open — accept any reasoned response.

periods.activity_title: Extract Analysis: Sven the Spaceman and the Warning

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect — Extract 1 (p.212): MCQ and SCR on Sven's abilities and zero-gravity evidence.
Let us think and reflect — Extract 2 (p.213): MCQ and SCR on the air-alarm crisis dialogue.

time_bands.activity: Read Extract 1 (p.212) aloud — the description of Sven collecting girders in free fall. Ask students to listen for specific phrases that signal zero gravity. Invite two or three students to identify those phrases.

Students work through the Extract 1 questions from "Let us think and reflect" (p.212): the MCQ on what Sven's job description reveals, the SCR on evidence of zero gravity, the assertion-reason MCQ, and the vocabulary replacement task. Discuss each answer as a class.

Read Extract 2 (p.213) aloud — the exchange where the narrator alerts Jim and the second alarm circuit is revealed unconnected. Then work through its questions: the fill-in on the narrator's reason for citing canaries, the SCR on Jim's dismissal, the MCQ on "shook Jim", and the SCR on the oxygen-bottle simile.

Lead a brief whole-class discussion: how does the phrase "pipe of peace" change the mood of the crisis moment? Take responses, then link the humour in Extract 2 to Arthur C. Clarke's wider narrative style noted in the story.

periods.teacher_notes: Having followed the story from Claribel's arrival through her collapse, students now analyse the two pivotal extracts closely. The assertion-reason MCQ in Extract 1 often catches students who conflate difficulty with impossibility; guide them to re-read the phrase "slow-motion, three-dimensional ballet" as evidence of challenge, not failure. The "pipe of peace" simile in Extract 2 carries the story's characteristic wry humour and rewards close attention.

periods.activity_title: Deeper Reading: Theme, Title and Humour

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.213): extended questions on alarm purpose, crew reaction, title, and Clarke's humour.

time_bands.activity: Read the story's closing paragraphs aloud (p.213) — the narrator's wry recommendation to future visitors who hear birdsong. Pause and ask: what tone does Clarke use here, and what does it suggest about his attitude toward the crew's near-death experience?

Work through the extended questions from "Let us think and reflect" (p.213) as a guided discussion: the purpose and failure of the alarm, how the crew's reaction to Claribel changes across the story, and the significance of the title. Invite extended student responses and push for textual evidence.

Focus on the question about science fiction and humour (p.213). Students share how Clarke blends serious consequences — almost dying — with a light narrative voice. Collect two or three responses on the board as a class summary.
Close by inviting one student to read the final line of the story aloud. Ask the class: does knowing the science make the story funnier or more serious? Accept brief responses.

periods.teacher_notes: Having worked through both extracts closely, students now step back to examine the whole narrative arc — how the crew's attitude to Claribel shifts from amusement to dependence. A common difficulty is students paraphrasing the plot when asked to "justify the title" rather than making an argument; model what a title-justification argument looks like before students attempt it. The question on Sven's hypothetical reflection (p.213) is left as an optional self-study prompt for interested students.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us listen (p.217): tick or cross five statements while listening to the Monika–Toby conversation.
Let us listen (p.218): fill five blanks with exact words from the conversation on second listening.

time_bands.activity: Set the context: tell students they will hear a conversation between Monika and Toby, a Martian stranded on Earth. Ask students to open p.217 and read the five true/false statements silently so they know what to listen for.

Read the Monika–Toby transcript aloud with expression — use distinct voices for each speaker. Students tick or cross each statement from "Let us listen" (p.217) as they listen. After the reading, take answers statement by statement and discuss briefly.

Read the transcript a second time, at a steady pace. Students fill the blanks from "Let us listen" (p.218) with exact words. After the reading, verify answers together, asking students to repeat the exact phrase they heard.

Lead a brief whole-class discussion: which of Toby's abilities — getting energy from the Sun, seeing through clouds, knowing what Monika ate — feels most surprising? Ask students to explain why in one sentence.
Connect the listening text to the main story: both feature a being from outside the norm who perceives something the others cannot. Ask students to identify the parallel in a single spoken sentence.

periods.teacher_notes: The transcript is performed live from p.249; students listen without reading the script, which is the intended exercise format. A common difficulty is students missing exact vocabulary in the fill-in task — the second reading should be deliberate and slightly slower, especially around "people and home", "Martians", "energy", and "chocolates". The thematic connection drawn at the end of the unit is an oral observation only and is not assessed.

periods.activity_title: Saying the Unsaid: Silent Letters and Space Advice

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us speak (p.—): read words aloud and identify silent letters in given and additional word lists.
Let us speak (p.—): paired role-play asking for and giving advice on solar system model and quiz prep.

time_bands.activity: Write the four words from "Let us speak" on the board — ballet, alarm, whistle, psychologist — and ask students to pronounce them. Model the correct pronunciation, then invite students to circle the silent letters. Extend to the additional ten words: receipt, debris, pneumonia, island, wreck, aisle, almond, campaign, foreign, fasten. Take turns around the class for each word.

Introduce the two situations from "Let us speak": making a solar system model and preparing for the Chandrayaan-3 quiz. Read the prompts for asking and giving advice together. Students work in pairs — one asks, one advises — then swap roles. Circulate and provide brief pronunciation and fluency feedback.

Invite two or three pairs to perform their advisory conversation for the class. After each pair, ask the audience: was the advice specific? Was the asking polite? Offer one point of praise and one of improvement per pair.

Close with a quick reflection: which silent-letter word from today surprised the class most? Take three hands. Note that silent letters often reflect the word's origin — a point to carry into dictionary exploration.

periods.teacher_notes: Students who have been reading about a space station will find the Chandrayaan-3 and solar system contexts in the speaking task naturally connected to the chapter's science theme. A common difficulty is students translating advice phrases literally from their home language, producing over-formal or stilted suggestions; model one genuine exchange before pairs begin. The silent-letter activity builds phonological awareness that supports both reading and writing across subjects.

periods.activity_title: Writing an Article: The Importance of Internet

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write (p.—): plan and draft a three-paragraph article titled "The Importance of Internet."

time_bands.activity: Introduce the article form using the points-to-remember from "Let us write": heading, writer's name, three-paragraph structure. Show on the board how a social media web of internet uses can be turned into paragraph points — brainstorm uses together (communication, research, entertainment, e-commerce).

Model a short Paragraph 1 together as a class — a general introduction to the internet. Discuss what makes an introduction engaging without being too vague. Students note down the model introduction and add one sentence of their own.

Students independently draft Paragraphs 2 and 3 in their exercise books. Paragraph 2 should explain uses with examples; Paragraph 3 should end with a thoughtful comment or quote. Circulate and offer individual guidance on structure, linking words, and avoiding repetition.

Peer-review round: students exchange books with a partner and read each other's article. Partner marks one strong sentence and suggests one improvement. Both students make at least one revision before the unit ends.

periods.teacher_notes: The article task begins and ends in this unit — drafting, peer response, and a first revision all happen here. A common difficulty is students listing uses without explaining significance; the guided opening and the peer-review prompt are designed to push toward explanation. Finished articles should be complete three-paragraph pieces by the end of this unit.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.214): match eight adjectives from the story to their noun collocations.
Let us learn (p.214): combine word pairs from two columns to form six merged words and give meanings.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the eight adjectives from "Let us learn" (p.214) — nagging, vague, delighted, narrow, sluggish, hushed, inexplicable, sheepish. Students match each to its noun from the list (path, worry, plan, look, reason, traffic, voices, expression). After checking answers, students return to the story text and underline sentences where these adjectives appear in context.

Introduce merged words using "intercom" as the model (internal + communication). Students combine the six pairs from Columns 1 and 2 to form motel, smog, sitcom, vlog, spork, webinar. For each merged word, students write its meaning in their own words before confirming with the class.

Quick consolidation: ask students to use two merged words in original sentences related to the theme of technology or space. Take three or four examples aloud. Close by noting that blending is a living feature of English — new merged words are coined regularly.

periods.teacher_notes: Vocabulary and grammar occupy their own unit here, isolated from other spines as required. The adjective-collocation task is anchored in the story's language, so students should be directed back to the text to confirm the collocations are genuine — "sluggish" and "sheepish" in particular carry the narrator's self-deprecating tone. The merged-word exercise rewards students who already know words like "smog" or "motel" without knowing their origin.

periods.activity_title: Future Time Reference: Will, Going To, and Simple Present

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.215): identify the time reference of "will" in the story's sentence; study the usage table.
Let us learn (p.216): fill eight blanks with correct future-time forms in varied sentences.

homework.task_brief: Let us learn (p.217): fill blanks with correct future-time verb forms in the AI paragraph passage.

time_bands.activity: Write the story sentence "It will mean that you're being doubly safeguarded" on the board. Ask students which time the word "will" refers to, then confirm: future. Introduce the usage table from "Let us learn" (p.215) — simple present for scheduled events, present progressive for arrangements, "going to" for intentions, "will" for predictions and offers. Work through one example of each form together.

Students complete the eight fill-in-the-blank sentences from "Let us learn" (p.216), choosing among the four future-time forms. After independent work, go through each sentence as a class — for each answer, ask a student to name the rule that applies (scheduled event, intention, prediction, etc.).

Write three original sentences on the board with incorrect or ambiguous future-time forms drawn from common errors (e.g., "I will go to the dentist next week — appointment already booked"). Students correct them and justify their correction with the usage rule.
Set homework from "Let us learn" (p.217): the AI paragraph with six future-time blanks. Remind students to apply the same rules from today's usage table.

periods.teacher_notes: The grammar focus here — future time reference — flows naturally from the story's closing line about what future visitors to the station "will" experience. A common difficulty is students over-using "will" where "going to" or simple present is more appropriate; the error-correction exercise in the third band is designed to surface and address this directly. The homework passage (p.217) extends the same grammar into a new context (AI and medicine) to check independent transfer.

periods.activity_title: Animals as Guardians: Exploring Beyond the Story

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us explore (p.—): read examples of animals sensing natural calamities and discuss if this is true.
Let us explore (p.—): work in groups to plan and construct a simple bird feeder from classroom materials.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the "Let us explore" investigation: animals sensing calamities. Read through the examples together — elephants and flamingos before the 2004 tsunami, oxen and geese before the Naples quake, migratory birds dodging storms, sharks sensing hurricanes. Ask each group to discuss one example and state whether the evidence convinces them, giving a reason.

Groups report back one at a time. Build a class list on the board: which animal examples feel most and least convincing? Invite cross-group challenge — can another group's reasoning change someone's view? Draw a parallel to Claribel in the story: the same principle of animal sensitivity, different context.

Introduce the bird feeder activity from "Let us explore". Groups plan their design briefly (shape, entry point, perch), then use available classroom materials — cardboard, chart paper, string — to begin construction. The feeder must be complete by the end of this unit.

Each group holds up their finished feeder. Ask one member per group to say in one sentence what the feeder is designed to attract and where they would place it. Close by connecting the care shown for birds here to Sven's care for Claribel.

periods.teacher_notes: The animal-sensing discussion and the bird-feeder construction are both completed within this unit — no material or draft is carried forward. Students who engaged deeply with Claribel's role as an early-warning system will find the animal-calamity examples a natural extension; the key pedagogical move is naming the shared principle (heightened biological sensitivity) across very different contexts. The bird feeder is kept simple and feasible within the available minutes — cardboard and chart paper are sufficient.

periods.activity_title: Whole-Chapter Synthesis: Science, Curiosity, and Claribel

time_bands.activity: Open with a whole-class discussion: what single sentence would you use to explain to a friend what "Feathered Friend" is about? Take eight or ten responses, write the best phrases on the board, and identify what elements — character, setting, theme — keep reappearing. This surfaces the chapter's central idea: low-tech solutions in high-tech environments.

Pose three synthesis questions for small-group discussion: (1) How does Clarke's humour — seen in the "pipe of peace" image and the narrator's wry closing recommendation — change how the story handles a near-death situation? (2) How does Sven's collocation of "sluggish" and "sheepish" after the crisis compare with how Jim reacts when the second alarm circuit is revealed? (3) If the story were set on Earth — say, in a coal mine — would the future-time language in the narrator's closing recommendation still feel as confident? Groups have a quick exchange, then one representative per group shares the most interesting point.

Individual writing task: students write a short paragraph (five to eight sentences) imagining they are Sven, writing a message back to Earth explaining why Claribel should be officially permitted aboard the station. They must use at least one future-time construction (will, going to, or simple present for a scheduled fact) and at least one of the adjectives from the story — nagging, sluggish, inexplicable, or sheepish — in a natural context. Drafting, self-review, and a final sentence are all done within this band.

Thematic contrast: connect the canary-in-the-coal-mine principle to the animal-sensing examples explored in the beyond-text investigation — elephants, flamingos, migratory birds. Ask students to name one similarity and one difference between Claribel's role and the animals in those examples. Take four or five spoken responses.

Close the chapter with Clarke's own final image: a space visitor hearing inexplicable birdsong and feeling reassured rather than alarmed. Ask the class: what does this ending say about the value of curiosity — Sven's, Claribel's, and the reader's own? Take two or three final responses and end the chapter there.

periods.teacher_notes: This synthesis unit assumes the chapter's content — the narrative, the grammar of future time reference, the adjective collocations, the beyond-text animal examples — has been read and discussed, though the specific path any class took to get here may differ. The short writing task in the third band begins and ends within this unit; students write as Sven and are done — nothing is carried forward. The thematic contrast in the fourth band works without any physical artefact: the discussion draws on what students know about the animal-sensing examples, not on any object they may or may not have made.

items.source_context: Sven smuggling Claribel aboard, her adaptation to zero gravity, the air-purifier failure, and the crew's shifting attitude.
items.item_stem: Which of the following best describes why Sven smuggled Claribel aboard the space station?

options.label: A
options.text: He had been asked by the station commander to conduct an official animal experiment.

options.label: B
options.text: He hoped Claribel would help him perform better at his construction work.

options.label: C
options.text: He wanted company because space station life was lonely.

options.label: D
options.text: He was curious to observe how a bird would behave in zero gravity.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Suggests the student is reading emotion into Sven's action without textual support.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Confuses Sven's personal scientific curiosity with an official sanctioned experiment.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Invents a practical motive for Claribel that the narrative does not support.

items.source_lo: Student infers character motivation and evaluates narrative evidence using a narrative text as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Sven smuggling Claribel aboard, her adaptation to zero gravity, the air-purifier failure, and the crew's shifting attitude.
items.item_stem: The narrator describes the crew's attitude toward Claribel as shifting over the course of the story. Trace this shift from the time Claribel is first discovered aboard the station to the moment the narrator makes his closing recommendation about birdsong to future visitors. What does this change reveal about what the crew came to value by the story's end?

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Initially the crew treated Claribel as an amusing secret mascot, hiding her from visiting VIPs; by the story's end, after she collapsed and revealed the failed air purifier, she was understood to be the station's living early-warning system. The shift reveals that the crew came to value low-tech biological sensitivity over expensive, failure-prone engineering.

items.source_context: Conversation between Monika and Toby the Martian: his diet, single eye, and ability to see through solids.
items.item_stem: Listen to the conversation between Monika and Toby. Decide whether each statement below is true or false.

options.text: Martians get their energy from eating plants.
Toby has one large eye in the centre of his face.
Toby misses his people and home.
Toby tells Monika she had a banana for breakfast.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer:
1. True — Toby says "I miss my people and home."
2. False — Martians get their energy from the Sun, not from plants.
3. True — Monika observes "I see only one big eye in the centre of your face."
4. False — Toby tells Monika she had an apple, not a banana, for breakfast.

items.source_context: Conversation between Monika and Toby the Martian: his diet, single eye, and ability to see through solids.
items.item_stem: After listening to the conversation, answer the following question in one or two sentences: Toby claims he can see certain things even with his eye closed. According to the conversation, what can Toby see, and what evidence in the conversation supports the idea that his vision is genuinely extraordinary?

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Toby says he can see beyond mountains, clouds, wood, and metals with his eye closed; he also correctly identifies a blue toy aeroplane in Monika's pocket and tells her that the apple she just ate is moving around in her stomach — two specific details that demonstrate his claim is genuine and not exaggerated.

Gives at least two specific, relevant suggestions about quiz preparation.

items.item_stem: In "Feathered Friend", a simple, low-cost creature turns out to be more valuable than expensive engineering. Write a short article (120–150 words) titled "Simple Solutions, Big Impact" in which you argue that simple ideas sometimes outperform complex ones. Draw on at least one idea from the story and one example from everyday life. Include an introduction, a body paragraph with examples, and a conclusion with a thoughtful comment.

items.item_stem:
The narrator of "Feathered Friend" closes the story by imagining a future visitor to the space station. Rewrite the following sentences by choosing the correct future-time form (simple present, "going to", or "will") from the options in brackets, and briefly explain the rule that governs your choice for sentence 2.
1. The annual maintenance inspection __________ (take place / is going to take place) next Tuesday — it is already on the station's official schedule.
2. If you hear birdsong on the station, it __________ (will mean / is meaning) you are doubly safeguarded.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. The annual maintenance inspection takes place next Tuesday — simple present is used because the event is a fixed scheduled fact. 2. It will mean you are doubly safeguarded — "will" is used because the narrator is making a general prediction or statement of consequence, not referring to a personal intention or a pre-arranged schedule.

items.source_context: Animals sensing natural calamities (tsunami, earthquake, storms) and the canary-in-the-coal-mine principle.
items.item_stem:
In the story, Claribel acts as a biological early-warning system for the space station crew. Read the following examples of animals reportedly sensing natural calamities and complete the task below.

• Before the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami, elephants in coastal areas moved to higher ground, and flamingos abandoned their nesting sites.
• Before the 1805 Naples earthquake, oxen, sheep, and geese became restless and refused to stay in their enclosures.

Select the statement that most accurately describes what these examples have in common with Claribel's role in the story.

options.label: A
options.text: Animals are more reliable warning systems than any human-made technology.

options.label: B
options.text: Animals behave unusually only when humans are present to observe them.

options.label: C
options.text: Animals can be trained by humans to detect specific dangers in advance.

options.label: D
options.text: Animals possess a biological sensitivity to environmental changes that humans lack.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Confuses instinctive biological sensitivity with deliberate trained behaviour.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Introduces a human-presence condition that neither the story nor the examples support.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Overstates the claim — the examples show animals are sometimes more sensitive, not always superior to all technology.

items.source_lo: Student connects the narrative's central idea to real-world phenomena and evaluates evidence across contexts using interdisciplinary exploration as the vehicle.

items.item_stem: Design a brief project plan (write in four to six sentences or bullet points) for an investigation titled "Nature's Warning Systems." Your plan should: identify one animal — other than a canary or the examples above — that you believe might sense danger before humans do; explain what danger it might detect and why its biology could make it sensitive to that danger; and describe one simple way a community or a scientific team could test this idea. Base your reasoning on what you have learned about how Claribel and the calamity-sensing animals responded to environmental changes.

expected_elements: Names a specific animal and links it to a plausible danger.
Gives a biological or behavioural reason for the animal's sensitivity.
Proposes a simple, testable observation method.
Connects the idea to the principle shown by Claribel or the calamity examples.
